Transcriptomic age with BulkFormer: overnight build

Data, protocol and first models built 2026-11-09 → 2026-11-10. Generated 2026-11-10 10:24 from the repository's parquet outputs.

MotivationDataMethodsResultsAchievementsProblems & decisionsNext steps

Motivation

Can a bulk-transcriptome foundation model read a donor's age from RNA-seq better than the classic linear clocks, across tissues, studies and even single-cell pseudobulk?

On 2026-11-04 the BulkFormer authors (Kang et al., Cell Systems 2026) released two models: BulkFormer-Atlas (242 M parameters, a 1,024-d CLS sample embedding from a fixed 4,096-gene panel; Atlas + HVG ranks first on the PRIMO patient-level bulk benchmark) and BulkFormer-Latest (154 M parameters, 768-d contextual gene embeddings over the full 19,973-gene coding transcriptome). Age is the textbook sample-level phenotype: every public RNA-seq sample with a donor age is a free label, and a good transcriptomic clock is useful for aging research, for disease "age acceleration", and as a stress test of how much biology a foundation model captures beyond batch and tissue.

Tonight's goal: build the data side (reproducible downloaders and parsers, a harmonised sample table with raw counts and donor ages), fix an evaluation protocol before any model, then climb a training ladder: linear baselines, frozen Atlas embeddings with probes, Atlas fine-tuning, and compare everything with published clocks (tAge, ClockBase) on the same held-out samples.

"eligible" = has an age, not excluded (tumour, cell line, stem cell / organoid, prenatal, single-cell run inside a bulk compendium, non-human). Disease samples stay eligible and are scored separately.

Sources

  • ARCHS4 human gene counts (file of 2026-11-06, 64 GB): ages parsed from GEO characteristics_ch1 (exact / binned / censored, months and weeks converted, gestational age and passage rejected).
  • GTEx v10 public release: read counts, 10-year age bins (exact age is controlled access, not used).
  • CELLxGENE Census LTS 2025-11-08: primary cells summed per donor × tissue (≥ 200 cells, ≥ 500k UMIs), 14 datasets incl. OneK1K, AIDA, the lung and liver atlases and PsychENCODE brain cohorts.
  • Terekhova et al. 2023 PBMC aging atlas (HCA copy): pseudobulk per tube, 166 donors aged 25–85; raw UMIs recovered from log1p-CP10k (100 % integral).
  • Bgee 15.2: curated healthy libraries with "NN-year-old" stages (most also in ARCHS4).
  • Labels only: 17 named aging cohorts (Fleischer 2018 fibroblasts, …) and the Shokhirev & Johnson 2021 compilation (6,471 curated samples), used to audit our age parser: 5,370 / 5,371 agree within 1 year.

Methods

Pipeline

rna-age fetch (resumable, parallel HTTP ranges, checksums) → rna-age parse (per-source samples.parquet + raw counts as gene × sample parquet parts) → rna-age merge (dedup, cohort labels, splits) → models. Everything is polars + parquet; heavy steps run as batch jobs.

Evaluation protocol (fixed before the first model)

  • Whole studies (GSE, Census dataset, Bgee experiment; GTEx donor) go to train / val / test (70/15/15) by a stable hash: no series or donor spans two splits. 99,559 samples carry a split.
  • Training set: bulk train split, healthy or unknown health status, exact ages; GTEx bins enter as midpoints in baselines and as an interval loss in fine-tuning.
  • Metrics: MAE, median AE, Pearson r, R², bias slope (regression to the mean); GTEx scored as interval hit rate and distance to the bin; per source, tissue, decade, health status and modality.
  • Transfer test: every pseudobulk sample predicted by models trained on bulk only.
  • Controls: tAge (relative clock, compared on age deltas within dataset × tissue strata) on the same samples, with and without the series it was trained on.

Training ladder

  1. Ridge / ElasticNet on log-CPM of highly variable genes chosen on train only (2k–20k genes; optional Horvath log-linear age target).
  2. BulkFormer-Atlas frozen CLS embeddings (fixed 4,096-gene panel chosen on train, fp16 on RTX 2080 Ti), ridge and MLP probes, CLS + HVG.
  3. Atlas fine-tuning: last N encoder blocks + regression head, Huber loss on exact ages + interval loss on GTEx bins, per-study sampling cap, early stopping on validation MAE.

Key findings

  1. Non-linear readouts win. Ridge on 20k log-CPM HVGs (+ Horvath target): test MAE 12.64; the same genes through a small MLP: 10.43; a 5-seed MLP ensemble: 10.44.
  2. More training data helps. Training on all health states (disease samples too): 7-model ensemble test MAE 9.52, r 0.793, validation MAE 9.00.
  3. Frozen BulkFormer-Atlas adds nothing. Ridge on Atlas CLS 15.45 vs ridge on its own 4,096 input genes 13.70; CLS + 20k HVG MLP 9.80 vs the HVG MLP ensemble 9.52: within the ±0.5-year run-to-run noise or worse.
  4. Frozen BulkFormer-Latest also adds nothing. On matched samples (16k training samples), an MLP on Latest's pooled embedding reaches test MAE 16.08 and on panel-pooled gene embeddings 16.08, vs 14.02 for the 20k-HVG MLP on the same samples.
  5. Gene-length TPM vs UMI pseudobulk. TPM features: best bulk test MAE 10.24 but transfer to 10x pseudobulk collapses (r 0.09); log-CPM keeps transfer at r 0.62. Atlas normalises every sample by gene length, which plausibly explains part of its weak transfer.
  6. Regression to the mean remains (test bias slope -0.33); a validation-fitted de-compression removes it but raises test MAE to 14.02.
  7. Fine-tuning BulkFormer-Atlas works when enough of it is unfrozen. Last 2 blocks + head: test MAE 13.67; last 4 blocks + head: 10.85 (r 0.763), with the best single-model pseudobulk transfer (MAE 13.81, r 0.66) after only 5 × 12k training samples. Trained on all health states it reaches 10.39 with the best pseudobulk transfer of any model (r 0.69), and averaged with the MLP ensemble it gives the best model overall: validation MAE 8.72, test MAE 9.26, r 0.816: the fine-tuned encoder is complementary to expression features.

What drives the ridge clock

Strongest "older" genes: EYA4, PTCHD4, NAP1L2, LMO3, ENSG00000244306, ZNF727, MIR34AHG, IGFBP3, CPS1, FIGN, DDO, NEFL. Strongest "younger" genes: RANBP17, ZNF518B, NEFH, HCG11, PODXL2, NRCAM, NKAPL, PIANP, SLC4A10, KLRB1, CD248, KCNG1. Known aging genes rank high (PTCHD4, LRRN3, CD248, the miR-34a and miR-29 host genes).

  • A reproducible pipeline: rna-age fetch | parse | merge | summary | baseline | embed | probe | finetune | tage | figures | report-tables | artifact.
  • Seven data sources parsed to one schema (samples, genes, raw counts), plus two label sources and one benchmark (LongevityBench GTEx tasks, flagged on our samples).
  • An age parser with 80+ tests built from real GEO strings; flags for tumour, cell line, stem cell, prenatal, single-cell runs.
  • A fixed evaluation protocol, run tracking (data/output/runs/, experiments.parquet), and a decision log (docs/experiments.md).
  • BulkFormer-Atlas CLS embeddings and panel inputs for every sample, an fp16 + attention-memory fix that lets Atlas run on 11 GB cards, and a resumable fine-tuning loop.
  • The tAge R package wrapped as a parquet-in / parquet-out step in an isolated R environment.

Problems & decisions

  • NCBI started answering its GEO download endpoint with a reCAPTCHA page: NCBI-generated counts are parked; we do not work around bot protection.
  • Synapse token on the cluster answered 401 (also with the official client): Terekhova counts came from the HCA copy, with raw UMIs recovered from log1p-CP10k (verified integral).
  • CELLxGENE Census SOMA reads stalled through the proxy: we used the same LTS release's h5ads over HTTPS; four chosen datasets were not in that release and were skipped to keep the release pinned.
  • ARCHS4 extraction ran out of memory twice (a 60 GB copy into a memory-backed temp dir; h5py fancy indexing over scattered columns): replaced by bounded dense windows, 75k samples in 4.5 minutes.
  • GPUs are 11 GB cards without native bf16: fp16 autocast (checked against fp32, cosine 1.000); Atlas passed an all-true attention mask that forced the full-matrix attention kernel, patched at runtime with identical maths.
  • Training filter bug caught before the first result: "healthy or unknown" silently dropped unknowns (polars null semantics), which would have cut training to 5,208 samples.
  • Choices made on Anton's behalf: GTEx bins as midpoints for baselines / interval loss for fine-tuning; healthy-or-unknown training set; per-study sampling cap; pseudobulk only as a transfer test; tAge compared on within-stratum deltas.
  • A 54 MB R diagnostics PDF slipped into three commits before it was ignored; history was not rewritten.

Next steps

  1. Longer, deeper Atlas fine-tuning. Unfreezing 4 blocks reached validation MAE ≈ 10.4 after only 5 × 12k samples and was still improving; a run with 6 blocks, 20k samples per epoch and all health states is in progress. Then all blocks with layer-wise learning-rate decay, 3 seeds.
  2. Fix the input normalisation for cross-assay use. Atlas divides every sample by gene length; for 10x UMI pseudobulk this is wrong. Prepare UMI data without the length step, or fine-tune with both assays and an assay token.
  3. Use all labelled data. Disease samples help (−0.8 y); add GTEx through the interval loss and pseudobulk as a separate domain with its own head or adapter.
  4. Beat the bar on the same split. The 7-model MLP ensemble on 20k log-CPM HVGs (test MAE in the Results tab) is what a fine-tuned BulkFormer must beat alone; combining both already helps.
  5. Close evaluation gaps. A pseudobulk test split (all pseudobulk studies landed in train/val), disease age acceleration with matched controls per study (not significant yet), and the regression to the mean.
  6. Data. NCBI-generated GEO counts (download page behind a reCAPTCHA from the cluster), more CELLxGENE datasets (tier 2), recount3 BioSample ages.
